title: Why Ceasefires Break Down
hook: A ceasefire stops the shooting. It does not make peace. The difference — and the danger — lies in everything a quick deal leaves out.
key_points: A ceasefire halts fighting; a durable peace also settles the dispute that caused it.
Fragile deals tend to omit enforcement, monitoring, and resolution of the core grievance.
Strong agreements build in real penalties for resuming war — automatic, reversible costs on whoever restarts it.
Without such 'credible commitments,' each side fears the other will rearm and strike first.
The 2026 US-Iran ceasefire is a live example of a pause that may not hold.
content_html: When two sides at war agree to stop shooting, it feels like the end of the story. Often it is only an intermission. A ceasefire is a pause in violence; a durable peace is something harder — an arrangement that also resolves the grievance behind the war and gives both sides reason not to pick the fight back up.
extra_html: Writing in The Conversation about the 2026 US-Iran ceasefire, international-politics scholar Monica Duffy Toft argues that the real danger of a quick deal is what it leaves out. A strong agreement, she explains, builds in real penalties for going back to war — automatic, reversible costs that fall on whoever restarts the fighting. That is a "credible commitment": each party can see that breaking the deal would hurt, so neither is tempted to rearm and strike first. A bare ceasefire that skips enforcement, monitoring, and the core dispute leaves mutual distrust fully intact, and distrust is what turns pauses back into wars. The broader lesson reaches well beyond any single conflict: stopping the violence is the easy part of peacemaking. Making the peace hold requires designing the incentives so that returning to war is the worse option for everyone.

related.title: War & Peace
related.hook: War is politics at its most extreme — organized violence between groups. Understanding why it happens, and how peace is kept, is central to the study of states.

related.title: Diplomacy & War
related.hook: States pursue their interests on a spectrum that runs from the conference table to the battlefield. Diplomacy and war are two ends of the same toolkit.

related.title: Precautionary Diplomacy
related.hook: Most treaties clean up a mess after it happens. A rarer kind acts first — banning commercial fishing in the Arctic before it even begins, to buy time for science.

flashcards.prompt: What is the difference between a ceasefire and a durable peace?
flashcards.back_html: A ceasefire only stops the fighting; a durable peace also resolves the underlying dispute and builds in ways to keep both sides from restarting.

flashcards.prompt: According to the analysis, what makes a ceasefire agreement strong rather than fragile?

choices.text: Built-in penalties — automatic, reversible costs on whoever resumes the fighting
Keeping the terms secret from the public
Leaving the hardest disputes unmentioned to avoid disagreement

flashcards.explanation_html: Political scientist Monica Duffy Toft argues a strong deal makes restarting war costly and automatic — a credible commitment that deters defection.

flashcards.prompt: Why can a ceasefire that 'leaves things out' be dangerous?

choices.text: Without enforcement, each side fears the other will rearm and strike first
Because ceasefires are illegal under international law
Because pausing a war always guarantees it resumes

flashcards.explanation_html: Missing monitoring and penalties leave mutual distrust intact, so the pause can collapse back into fighting rather than mature into peace.
